verdict_reasoning: Both bugs are reported by users and reproduced by a reviewer, and 0002 uses the existing relationOids invalidation channel. The surviving objections are fixable design points about the 0004 lock: its duration and back-branch status (standards-compat-1), its PL/pgSQL-only scope (standards-compat-2) and its effect on hot standby replay (replication-ondisk-1). None questions the goal. A committer who knows locking and the plan cache has to judge the new blocking behavior.

brief.title: Fix stale plans and a race for SETOF functions after ALTER TYPE
brief.problem: PL/pgSQL functions that use RETURN QUERY over a non-inlined SETOF function returning a named composite fail with "structure of query does not match function result type" after ALTER TYPE ... ADD ATTRIBUTE or ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN. Users reported it. A second form of the failure happens when a concurrent transaction alters the type while RETURN QUERY is running, and CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION does not help there.
brief.proposed_design: The planner records the typrelid of a named composite returned by each RTE_FUNCTION in the plan's relation dependencies, so the relcache invalidation that ALTER TYPE sends marks cached plans stale. PL/pgSQL takes AccessShareLock on that typrelid at function entry for SETOF functions returning a named composite, and holds it to transaction end. A concurrent ALTER TYPE or ALTER TABLE then waits behind the running call.
user_visible_surface: Cached and prepared plans that scan SETOF functions returning a composite (also through a domain) are replanned after ALTER TYPE, as the new ALTER TYPE doc paragraph states.
A running SETOF PL/pgSQL call holds AccessShareLock on its composite return type until transaction end, so ALTER TYPE/ALTER TABLE on that type blocks.
author_claims: Bug 1 reproduces in a single session and the setrefs.c change makes the second call return the new 3-column shape.
Bug 2 reproduces reliably only with injection points; an included TAP test covers it.
The lock mirrors how table scans hold AccessShareLock to pin the schema for the statement.
Both bugs still reproduce on the newest minor releases.
brief.thread_state: Surya Poondla reproduced both bugs, confirmed relationOids is the right invalidation channel, and sent test and comment fixes that v2 addresses. Heikki Linnakangas is a listed reviewer but has not posted; the author asked again on 2026-11-10 to move the fixes forward.
unclear: The material does not say whether the fixes are meant for back branches or only master.
The material does not measure the cost of extra plan dependencies or of the new lock on each function call.
The material does not discuss deadlock or lock-wait risk for DDL that now blocks behind long transactions holding the new lock.
The material does not say whether other PLs or SQL-language functions have the same race.
CFbot reported a rebase need on 2026-09-08; the thread does not show a newer version.

prior_attempts.title: Support prepared statement invalidation when result or argument types change
prior_attempts.quote: What if the client has previously done a Describe Statement on the prepared statement? We have no mechanism for notifying it that that information is now falsified.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane called the change a wire protocol break: a client that already ran Describe Statement has no way to learn that the result description is now wrong, and the error exists to prevent that. Shay Rojansky noted that the Npgsql driver caches RowDescriptions. The author agreed and withdrew the patch until the protocol has a way to signal a new RowDescription, for which he needs the separate protocol-version work.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 removed the "cached plan must not change result type" check so clients would get a new RowDescription. This proposal only adds the composite typrelid to plan dependencies and does not change what is reported to clients, so the reason P2 was withdrawn does not apply.

objections.title: New lock changes ALTER TYPE blocking for existing users, mainly if backpatched
objections.failure_scenario: An application keeps a transaction open after calling a SETOF PL/pgSQL function. A deploy script runs ALTER TYPE on the standalone composite type and waits on its AccessExclusiveLock. Every new call to any SETOF function returning that type then queues behind it, and the script that used to finish at once now stalls the application.
objections.argument: Patch 0004 takes AccessShareLock at function entry and holds it to transaction end. Message #1 justifies it as keeping the row shape stable within one statement, which is a shorter span than the lock covers. Today, ALTER TYPE on a standalone composite does not wait for function callers, so this is a new blocking contract. The material does not say whether the fix targets back branches, where such a change in locking behavior would surprise users after a minor upgrade.
objections.author_must_show: Is the lock meant for back branches, and why must it last to transaction end instead of the end of the calling statement?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 states that the lock lasts to transaction end, while its stated goal is a stable row shape within one statement. The thread does not say whether 0004 targets back branches, and no message weighs the DDL wait.

objections.title: Race fix covers only PL/pgSQL, other function languages keep the race
objections.failure_scenario: A user ports the reported function to a SQL-language or PL/Python SETOF function returning the same composite. A concurrent ALTER TYPE plus CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION commits mid-call. The user hits the same row-shape mismatch error that the release notes say is fixed.
objections.argument: Message #1 places the root cause in plpgsql_estate_setup(), and patch 0004 touches only pl_exec.c. The condition it guards against is a tuple descriptor captured at call start and then replanned against a changed type. That condition is not specific to PL/pgSQL. A committer would likely ask for a fix in the common function-call or SRF path, or for a stated reason why other languages are safe.
objections.author_must_show: Do SQL-language functions and other PLs returning SETOF a named composite have the same race, and if so, where would a common fix go?

critic.reasoning: Patch 0004 touches only pl_exec.c, and the thread does not say whether SQL-language functions or other PLs have the same race. A reason for a PL/pgSQL-only fix is a fair request.

objections.title: New lock on typrelid adds hot standby replay conflicts
objections.failure_scenario: A reporting standby runs a long transaction that calls a SETOF PL/pgSQL function returning planinv_ct. The primary runs ALTER TYPE planinv_ct ADD ATTRIBUTE. Replay of the logged AccessExclusiveLock on typrelid now waits behind the standby's new AccessShareLock, so replay stalls up to max_standby_streaming_delay and then cancels the query.
objections.argument: 0004 takes AccessShareLock on typrelid at function entry and holds it to transaction end (message #1). Standbys replay AccessExclusiveLock records, so this creates a conflict that did not exist before, on standbys that never run the DDL. This copies how table scans behave, which lowers the concern, but the thread covers only the primary. If the fix goes to back branches, standby operators would see new replay lag or new query cancels after a minor update.
objections.author_must_show: How does the new lock behave on a hot standby during replay of ALTER TYPE, and is that change acceptable in a minor release if this is backpatched?

critic.reasoning: Standbys replay AccessExclusiveLock records, so a standby transaction holding the new lock on a standalone composite's typrelid is a new replay conflict. Table scans behave the same way, which lowers the concern, but the thread does not discuss standbys or back branches.

refuted.title: New lock lets any caller block DDL on a table they cannot read
refuted.failure_scenario: A role with no SELECT on table t creates a PL/pgSQL function returning setof t, calls it inside begin, and leaves the transaction open. The owner's alter table t queues for AccessExclusiveLock, and every later query on t waits behind it. The owner finds out when the application stalls.
refuted.argument: In message #1 the patch calls LockRelationOid on the typrelid at function entry and holds the lock to transaction end, and nothing says a privilege is checked first. Table rowtypes count as named composites, and type USAGE is normally granted to PUBLIC, so the caller needs only EXECUTE on a function, which may be one they wrote. Postgres has worked to stop unprivileged roles from locking relations they have no rights on, and the material does not argue that this lock stays within that rule.
refuted.author_must_show: Which privilege on the typrelid relation must the caller hold before the new lock is taken, and does a role without SELECT on the table get the lock today with v2?

critic.reasoning: Parse analysis already takes AccessShareLock on a table before any privilege check and holds it to transaction end. A role without SELECT can hold the same lock today with `begin; prepare p as select * from t;`, so 0004 adds no new capability.

refuted.title: Race fix covers PL/pgSQL only, not other SETOF callers
refuted.failure_scenario: A user hits the same mid-call mismatch from an SQL-language SRF, PL/Python return_next or a C SRF while another session runs ALTER TYPE. The plpgsql_estate_setup() lock does not run there, so the error stays. Each later PL needs its own copy of the lock, and nothing fails if one is missed.
refuted.argument: Message #1 places the lock in plpgsql_estate_setup(), so the rule "row shape is stable for the statement" holds only for one PL. The material does not say whether other PLs or SQL functions have the same race. A committer would likely ask for the lock at a shared point, such as the function call setup in the executor, or for a reason why PL/pgSQL is the only affected language.
refuted.author_must_show: Do SQL-language and other PL SETOF functions have the same race, and why is pl_exec.c the right place for the lock instead of shared executor code?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2, which states the same PL/pgSQL-only concern with a cleaner scenario.

refuted.title: New lock held to transaction end changes DDL wait behavior
refuted.failure_scenario: A long reporting transaction calls a SETOF PL/pgSQL function once. A deploy then runs ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN on the returned rowtype's table and waits. Every new caller of that function then queues behind the AccessExclusiveLock request, so the application stalls. The operator finds this only after a minor-release upgrade, if the fix is backpatched.
refuted.argument: Message #1 takes the lock at function entry and keeps it until transaction end, which is longer than the RETURN QUERY window it protects. The CF entry is tagged Bugfix, but the material does not say whether the lock change is meant for back branches. Adding a new lock that blocks DDL in a minor release changes behavior users can see. No message weighs the lock-wait or deadlock risk.
refuted.author_must_show: Is 0004 meant for back branches, and why must the lock last until transaction end instead of only for the duration of the call?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which covers the same lock duration and back-branch question.

refuted.title: Point fixes may conflict with ongoing tuple descriptor versioning work
refuted.failure_scenario: The setrefs.c dependency and the PL/pgSQL lock go into master. Then broader tuple descriptor and attribute versioning work lands, and the project must keep both mechanisms, or later remove a user-visible lock and a documented invalidation rule.
refuted.argument: Message #5 mentions work on tuple descriptors and attribute versioning in the new release, and says both bugs still reproduce after it. No message says how the two efforts relate. The patch documents a new invalidation promise in alter_type.sgml, which commits the project to keep that behavior. No committer who knows plancache or PL/pgSQL has posted. Heikki is listed as a reviewer but is silent.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the recent tuple descriptor versioning work give a more general place to fix these bugs, and has anyone working on it reviewed this approach?

critic.reasoning: Message #5 says the versioning work is already released and both bugs still reproduce, and nothing in the thread shows a conflict with it. The setrefs.c change uses the existing relationOids mechanism, and reviewer silence belongs under committability.

refuted.title: Bug 2 lock puts a cost on every caller to fix a rare race
refuted.failure_scenario: A site calls a SETOF PL/pgSQL function inside a long reporting transaction. A deploy then runs ALTER TYPE on its return type and waits for AccessExclusiveLock. Every new call of the function queues behind that waiting DDL, and the site sees a stall it did not have before.
refuted.argument: Bug 1 has user reports and a single-session reproducer (message #1), so its demand is shown. Bug 2 is one user report, and message #1 says it reproduces reliably only with injection points. The 0004 lock applies to every call of every SETOF PL/pgSQL function that returns a named composite, so all of those users pay, while only sites that run concurrent ALTER TYPE plus CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION gain. The thread does not weigh this trade, and it gives no measurements.
refuted.author_must_show: How often do users hit the mid-call race outside injection points, and what does the new per-call lock cost in lock waits and call overhead?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1; the failure scenario is the same DDL wait. Message #1 shows users hit the race in production even after adding CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION, so the demand part does not hold.

precedents_retrieved.title: allow mix of composite and scalar variables in target list
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the PL/pgSQL parser check that rejects a row (composite) variable inside a multiple-item INTO list. That inconsistency would also limit later changes for backward-compatibility reasons. He asked for new notation that removes the ambiguity, and Robert Haas's support for the 1:1 matching did not settle it. precedents_retrieved.title: Relax transactional restrictions on ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE (redux).
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Relax transactional restrictions on ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE (redux).
Reverted commit(s): Revert to 9.6 treatment of ALTER TYPE enumtype ADD VALUE.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Originally committed as 15bc038f (plus some follow-ups), this was
reverted in 28e07270 due to a problem discovered in parallel
workers.  This new version corrects that problem by sending the
list of uncommitted enum values to parallel workers.

Here follows the original commit message describing the change:

To prevent possibly breaking indexes on enum columns, we must keep
uncommitted enum values from getting stored in tables, unless we
can be sure that any such column is new in the current transaction.

Formerly, we enforced this by disallowing ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE
from being executed at all in a transaction block, unless the target
enum type had been created in the current transaction.  This patch
removes that restriction, and instead insists that an uncommitted enum
value can't be referenced unless it belongs to an enum type created
in the same transaction as the value.  Per discussion, this should be
a bit less onerous.  It does require each function that could possibly
return a new enum value to SQL operations to check this restriction,
but there aren't so many of those that this seems unmaintainable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
Reverted commit(s): Don't allow GetTransactionSnapshot() in logical decoding
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 1585ff7387 changed GetTransactionSnapshot() to throw an error
if it's called during logical decoding, instead of returning the
historic snapshot. I made that change for extra protection, because a
historic snapshot can only be used to access catalog tables while
GetTransactionSnapshot() is usually called when you're executing
arbitrary queries. You might get very subtle visibility problems if
you tried to use the historic snapshot for arbitrary queries.

There's no built-in code in PostgreSQL that calls
GetTransactionSnapshot() during logical decoding, but it turns out
that the pglogical extension does just that, to evaluate row filter
expressions. You would get weird results if the row filter runs
arbitrary queries, but it is sane as long as you don't access any
non-catalog tables. Even though there are no checks to enforce that in
pglogical, a typical row filter expression does not access any tables
and works fine. Accessing tables marked with the user_catalog_table =
true option is also OK.

To fix pglogical with row filters, and any other extensions that might
do similar things, revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return a
historic snapshot during logical decoding.

To try to still catch the unsafe usage of historic snapshots, add
checks in heap_beginscan() and index_beginscan() to complain if you
try to use a historic snapshot to scan a non-catalog table. We're very
close to the version 18 release however, so add those new checks only
in master.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert my ill-considered change that made formrdesc not insert the correct relation rowtype OID into the relcache entries it builds.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Revert my ill-considered change that made formrdesc not insert the correct relation rowtype OID into the relcache entries it builds.  This ensures that catcache copies of the relation tupdescs will be fully correct. While the deficiency doesn't seem to have any effect in the current sources, we have been bitten by not-quite-right catcache tupdescs before, so it seems like a good idea to maintain the rule that they should be right.

roaster_notes.note: The only listed precedent, P2, was withdrawn because it would change the RowDescription that a client had already cached. This proposal keeps the result-type check, so that reason does not apply. The thread cites no earlier discussion of the same fix.
The plan invalidation in patch 0002 follows existing relcache dependency practice, and the thread checked that it uses the right invalidation channel. No standards objection to that part.

The plan-dependency fix (0002) changes only in-memory plan cache state. It does not touch on-disk format, WAL records, catalogs, the wire protocol or struct layouts, so it raises no concern from this angle. [P2] is about RowDescription on the wire and does not apply to SPI plans inside PL/pgSQL.
The plan invalidation change in 0002 has no privilege or exposure aspect that I can see.
The bug and the planner fix in 0002 look sound in broad strokes. A reviewer reproduced both bugs and confirmed relationOids is the right invalidation channel.

Postgres has no existing feature that does this job, so this angle raises nothing. For bug 1, running create or replace function on the inner SRF works around the stale plan by hand, but a manual step after every alter type is not a fix for wrong cached-plan behaviour. For bug 2, message #1 shows that create or replace function does not help, and lock table cannot lock a standalone composite type. [P2] covers result-type changes of prepared statements at the protocol level, not this RETURN QUERY case.

Bug 1 shows real demand: users reported it, it reproduces in one session, and a reviewer confirmed it (messages #1, #2). The only demand concern is the cost of the bug 2 lock compared with its narrow benefit.
